newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala growth forecasts flawed - think tank.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala growth forecasts flawed - think tank.

text.p: The Guatemalan central bank is using outdated methodology in calculating Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and inflation that leads to overly optimistic results in both, a prominent local think tank said Thursday.

"The statistics related with the consumer price index and those used to estimate the growth of the gross domestic product are not credible," economist Pablo Rodas, of the Research and Social Studies Association (ASIES), told Reuters.

Banco de Guatemala, as the country's central bank is called, predicts 1996 GDP growth of 3.3 percent and inflation of 10 percent, but Rodas said ASIES estimates GDP growth of between 1.65 and 2.5 percent and inflation several points higher than 10 percent forecast.
The difference, he said, is largely due to methodology.

The central bank's Monthly Economic Activity Index, used to predict the GDP, is flawed, he said. The index does not include the financial sector or the textile assembly industry, and it doesn't reflect seasonal fluctuations in Guatemala's sizable agricultural sector.
In order to improve the index, the bank must conduct a monthly poll of business and industry, asking about inventory, employment and other factors instead of sales alone, Rodas said.
Banco de Guatemala began the year predicting 4.9 percent growth, but has revised the number downward several times. Most recently the bank projected a 3.3 percent growth rate this year.

The slow-down in Guatemala's economy, which grew at 4.0 percent in 1994 and 4.9 percent in 1995, has been the subject of heated debate all year. Many business leaders claim the economy is in a recession, not just a slowdown.

Rodas said real inflation would probably be "several points" higher if the National Statistics Institute were to update the structure of its consumer price index, which is based on a 15- year-old poll.
According to Rodas, the index is not weighted correctly and does not reflect the current proportions of spending in the average Guatemalan household.
He said that, for example, education costs Guatemalans more than 2.4 percent of their spending, which is the weight it is given in the index.
Changing the weight given education would affect the inflation rate because "the cost of education every year has gone up much more than the general inflation rate," said Rodas.
In addition, the 42.3 percent weight given to food spending is too high, said Rodas.
